Major Node.js versions enter Current release status for six months, which gives library authors time to add support for them. After six months, releases after 26 move to Active LTS status and are ready for general use. LTS release status is “long-term support”, which typically guarantees that critical bugs will be fixed for a total of 30 months. Production applications should only use Active LTS or Maintenance LTS releases.

Node.js is part of the [OpenJS Foundation’s Ecosystem Sustainability Program](https://openjsf.org/ecosystem-sustainability-program) (ESP).

Commercial support is available for some deprecated LTS versions of Node.js through the [HeroDevs Never-Ending Support](https://www.herodevs.com/support/node-nes) initiative. Commercial support for Node.js is also available through [TuxCare’s Endless Lifecycle Support](https://tuxcare.com/endless-lifecycle-support/nodejs-eol-support/).

More information is available on the [Node.js website](https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases).

You should be running one of the supported release numbers listed above in the rightmost column.

node --version

Major Node.js versions enter *Current* release status for six months, which gives library authors time to add support for them.
Historically (up to Node.js 26), odd-numbered releases (9, 11, etc.) become unsupported after six months, and even-numbered releases (10, 12, etc.) move to *Active LTS* status and are ready for general use.
Starting with Node.js 27, the release cycle will be annual and every major version will move to *LTS* status after its six-month *Current* phase (and six additional months of *Alpha* phase).
*LTS* release status is "long-term support", which typically guarantees that critical bugs will be fixed for a total of 30 months.
Production applications should only use *Active LTS* or *Maintenance LTS* releases.

Full details regarding the Node.js release schedule are available [on GitHub](https://github.com/nodejs/release#release-schedule).

The Node.js website provides several non-interactive installation methods on the Downloads page, including command-line interfaces (CLIs), operating system (OS) package managers (e.g., `brew`), and Node.js version managers (e.g., `nvm`).

To highlight and promote community contributions, the Node.js project introduced a revised Downloads page categorizing installation methods as either “Recommended” or “Community.” This provides users with increased flexibility and choice, while keeping a short, curated list for those who want a straightforward starting point.

Anyone can propose a new installation method for the Downloads page. While the Node.js project makes the final call on what gets listed, proposals are evaluated against the criteria below.

“Recommended” methods are selected for their reliability and close alignment with official releases, and meet the following criteria (in addition to all “Community” criteria):

- “Recommended” methods make new Node.js releases available simultaneously with the official release.
- “Recommended” methods use the official Node.js binaries without alteration, only building from source when pre-built binaries are not available.
- “Recommended” methods allow developers to install and use multiple versions of Node.js on a system concurrently.
- “Recommended” methods have a close relationship with the Node.js project, including direct communication channels.

“Community” methods are additional installation methods also available on the Downloads page, and meet the following criteria:

- “Community” methods must support all currently supported, non-End-of-Life (EOL) Node.js versions.
- “Community” methods must function on at least one officially supported Operating System (OS), and must not be limited to a subset of OS distributions or versions.
- “Community” methods must be free to use and open source, must not be sold as a commercial product, and must not be a paid service.",
